segments.t: In the kitchen, waiter Kostya rushes to Chef Viktor Barinov with terrifying news. A guest at table seven, suspected of being a secret food critic, has just sent back her salad, complaining about the sour dressing. Listen to their panicked conversation in Russian first, and then we will examine each sentence.
Шеф, внимание! На кухне чрезвычайная ситуация.
И у меня отказ от салата!
Now, let us examine the vocabulary and phrasing of this dramatic kitchen crisis.
Шеф, внимание! На кухне чрезвычайная ситуация.
'Chef, attention! There is an emergency in the kitchen.' Kostya bursts into the workspace with urgent news.
'Kostya, what happened in the dining room?' Chef Barinov uses the perfective verb meaning 'happened' to focus on the single completed result, pairing it with 'dining room'.
'A presumed restaurant critic has been spotted!' Kostya uses the perfective verb meaning 'detected' to focus on the single completed result, pairing it with 'presumed' and 'restaurant'.
'She is sitting at table seven.' Kostya identifies the exact location of the threat.
И у меня отказ от салата!
'And I have a refusal of the salad!' Kostya uses the classic Russian possession phrasing — literally 'at me' rather than a verb meaning 'to have', combining 'refusal' with 'salad'.
'What do you mean a refusal? My perfect salad?' Viktor gasps in personal and professional shock.
'She sent the plate back, chef.' Kostya uses the perfective verb meaning 'returned' to focus on the single completed result, pairing it with 'plate' and 'back'.
'Which table? Definitely the seventh?' Viktor demands precise confirmation of the customer.
'Yes, a stern lady in glasses.' Kostya describes the appearance of the difficult diner.
'What exactly did she dislike?' Chef Barinov delivers a punchy one-word reaction built around the Russian word meaning 'pleased'.
'She said that the sauce is too sour.' Kostya uses the perfective verb meaning 'she said' to focus on the single completed result, pairing it with 'sauce' and 'too'.
'This is a signature recipe of haute cuisine!' Russian omits the present-tense verb 'to be' here, linking 'signature' directly with 'recipe', combining 'signature' with 'recipe' and 'high'.
'Chef, she has already opened a notepad.' Kostya puts the word for 'already' together with 'opened' and 'notepad' in a crisp, natural spoken turn of phrase.

'I personally will make dessert for her!' Viktor vows to win over the critic with sweet culinary mastery. Now, let us listen to the complete scene again to practice your comprehension. Now let's listen to the whole conversation again from start to finish.
